# Literate programming and reproducible science

## The problem: your paper and your analysis drift apart

::: incremental
-   The classic workflow: analyze *over here* (scripts, console), write *over there* (Word), and hand-carry numbers and figures between them
-   Every revision re-opens the gap: figure version five in a version-three draft, a mean in the text the code no longer produces, methods that describe last month's analysis
-   Scientific bugs are usually **silent** - nothing crashes when the pasted number is stale
-   An analysis you cannot regenerate is one you cannot defend - to reviewers, collaborators, or yourself in six months
:::

## Literate programming: the document *is* the analysis

> "Instead of imagining that our main task is to instruct a computer what to do, let us concentrate rather on explaining to human beings what we want a computer to do." - Donald Knuth, *Literate Programming* (1984)

::: incremental
-   One plain-text document holds the **prose, the code, and the results** - rendering re-runs everything from data to figures
-   The numbers *in your sentences* are computed, not typed, so they can never disagree with your data
-   Your methods become **self-documenting**; inconsistencies between what you say and what you do become visible
-   You already live this: our lab notebook templates, the companion notebooks, this very slide deck and the course book are all Quarto
:::

## Reproducibility has a policy behind it: FAIR

::: incremental
-   Funders (including NIH's data management and sharing policy) expect research outputs to be **FAIR**:
    -   **F**indable - deposited somewhere with a persistent identifier, not "available upon request"
    -   **A**ccessible - retrievable by standard tools, no special software or permission maze
    -   **I**nteroperable - open, documented formats (tidy `.tsv` and `.qmd`, not binary one-offs)
    -   **R**eusable - enough documentation and provenance that someone else can actually use it
-   Literate documents are FAIR practice: plain text any tool can read, methods that travel *with* the analysis, one source anyone can re-run
-   The arc of the rest of the course: today the **documents** → Week 9 the **environments** → Week 10 **sharing it all** on GitHub
:::

# Quarto: one source, many outputs

## Markdown, then Quarto

-   **Markdown**: a lightweight plain-text formatting language

    ``` markdown
    **bold**   *italic*   `code`   [a link](https://quarto.org)

    # Big header
    ## Smaller header

    -   a bullet
    1.  a numbered item
    ```

-   **Quarto** extends Markdown into a scientific publishing system: the same text, plus a **YAML header** and **executable code chunks**

-   One `.qmd` source can render to HTML, PDF, Word, slides, websites, and books - this deck, the course site, and the course book are all Quarto

## Anatomy of a `.qmd`: three ingredients

```` markdown
---
title: "My Analysis"        # 1. YAML header: document settings;
author: "Your Name"         #    format picks the output
format: html                #    (html, pdf, docx, revealjs, ...)
---

## A section heading

Ordinary Markdown prose.    # 2. Markdown text

```{{r}}
#| label: my-first-chunk    # 3. Code chunks, run at render time
x <- 5                      #    {{r}} runs through knitr,
print(x^2)                  #    {{python}} through Jupyter -
```                         #    same chunk options in both
````

-   `---` fences the YAML header; back ticks fence the code
-   Mixing R and Python in one file works too (via `reticulate`) - details in [Ch. 16](../book/chapters/16-quarto-documents.html)

## Rendered, the chunks look like this

::: panel-tabset
### R

```{r}
#| label: lec07-first-chunk-r
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

x <- 5
print(x^2)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: lec07-first-chunk-py
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

x = 5
print(x**2)
# 25
```
:::

-   Code first, output underneath - Quarto ran the code while rendering
-   Run chunks interactively as you write: the arrows on each chunk in Positron, or `Cmd/Ctrl + Enter` line by line

## Chunk options control what the reader sees

Options go *inside* the chunk with `#|` - identical in every language:

```` markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: fig-stiffness
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Stiffness by hydrogel concentration"
boxplot(compression ~ hydrogel_concentration, data = mydata)
```
````

| Option           | Effect                                        |
|------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `echo: false`    | Run the code, **hide** the code (manuscripts!) |
| `eval: false`    | **Show** the code, don't run it               |
| `include: false` | Run it, show **nothing** (setup chunks)       |
| `fig-cap:`       | Figure caption                                |
| `label: fig-...` | Makes the figure numbered and referenceable   |

::: callout-tip
Set document-wide defaults in the YAML under `execute:`; override per chunk only where needed.
:::

## Inline code: sentences that cannot go stale

```` markdown
```{{r}}
#| include: false
stickle <- read_tsv("data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv")
```

We measured `r knitr::inline_expr("ncol(stickle) - 3")` genes in
`r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(stickle)")` fish (@fig-gene1).
````

-   Renders as: "We measured 600 genes in 80 fish (Figure 1)."
-   Re-run with more fish next month → the sentence updates itself
-   This is the single biggest practical win of literate programming

## Rendering: one command, any format

``` bash
quarto render report.qmd              # the format named in the YAML
quarto render report.qmd --to pdf     # PDF (needs TinyTeX installed once)
quarto preview report.qmd             # live preview on every save
quarto render                         # a whole project or website
```

-   In **Positron**: the Preview button, or `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + K`

-   List several formats in the YAML and render them all from one source:

    ``` yaml
    format:
      html: default
      pdf: default
      docx: default
    ```

| Output type | Formats |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **Documents** | HTML, PDF (via LaTeX), Word |
| **Presentations** | RevealJS (these slides!), PowerPoint, Beamer |
| **Websites and books** | HTML (all of our class material!) |

## Callouts and cross-references

``` markdown
::: {.callout-tip title="Pro tip"}
Five callout types: note, tip, warning, important, caution.
:::

![Scaffold under SEM](images/scaffold.png){#fig-sem width=60%}

As shown in @fig-sem, the pores are uniform.
```

Label it once, reference it with `@`, and Quarto numbers everything on every render:

| Type | Label | Reference |
|:-----------|:----------------------------------------|:---------------|
| Figure | `#| label: fig-name` or `{#fig-name}` | `@fig-name` |
| Table | `#| label: tbl-name` or `{#tbl-name}` | `@tbl-name` |
| Equation | `$$ ... $$ {#eq-name}` | `@eq-name` |
| Section | `## Heading {#sec-name}` | `@sec-name` |

## Mathematics: LaTeX between dollar signs

-   Single `$` for **inline** math, double `$$` for **display** math on its own line:

    ``` markdown
    The area, $A = \pi r^2$, appears inline, whereas

    $$Pr(Y=r) = \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^r}{r!}$$

    gets its own centered line.
    ```

    The area, $A = \pi r^2$, appears inline, whereas $$Pr(Y=r) = \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^r}{r!}$$ gets its own centered line.

-   Works identically in HTML, PDF, Word, and slides

## Numbered equations are cross-references too

``` markdown
$$
\mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
$$ {#eq-se}

The standard error (@eq-se) shrinks with sample size.
```

$$
\mathrm{SE} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
$$ {#eq-se}

The standard error (@eq-se) shrinks with sample size.

::: callout-tip
Every Greek letter, operator, matrix, and aligned multi-line derivation you will ever need: [Ch. 17](../book/chapters/17-latex-basics.html) and [App. G](../book/chapters/appendix-G-latex.html). You'll see matrices and aligned equations live in the manuscript demo.
:::

## Citations: a `.bib` file and `@key`

``` bibtex
@article{knuth1984literate,
  author  = {Knuth, Donald E.},
  title   = {Literate Programming},
  journal = {The Computer Journal},
  year    = {1984}
}
```

``` markdown
---
bibliography: references.bib
csl: nature.csl        # optional: any journal's citation style
---

Knuth introduced literate programming [@knuth1984literate].
```

-   Zotero and Google Scholar export BibTeX entries directly
-   Quarto formats every citation *and* builds the reference list automatically; swap the `.csl` file to re-style them all for a different journal

# Three demos - same skeleton, three outputs

## Demo 1: slides (`example_slides.qmd`)

**`format: revealjs`** - a deck like this one, from one `.qmd`.

Watch for:

-   `##` = new slide, `#` = section divider
-   `::: incremental` and `. . .` to reveal content stepwise
-   Two-column layouts, executed R chunks, stepwise code highlighting
-   Tabsets, callouts, and math on slides
-   Speaker notes (press **S**) and the overview (press **O**)

## Demo 2: a manuscript (`example_manuscript.qmd`)

**`format: pdf`** - a Science/Nature-style article, LaTeX without writing LaTeX.

Watch for:

-   Scholarly YAML: authors, **affiliations**, ORCID, corresponding author, abstract, keywords
-   `echo: false` - readers see results, never code
-   Inline and display math, **numbered equations**, and `@fig-`/`@tbl-`/`@eq-`/`@sec-` cross-references throughout
-   Superscript citations from `example_manuscript.bib` + `nature.csl`, reference list built for free
-   Companion files travel with the source: `.bib`, `.csl`, `title.tex`

::: callout-important
Your **term project report** should start from this skeleton - create the `.qmd` this week.
:::

## Demo 3: a website (`example_website.zip`)

**A folder, not a file** - `_quarto.yml` turns it into a project; every `.qmd` becomes a page.

Watch for:

-   `_quarto.yml`: the navbar, theme, and `output-dir: docs`
-   An `about:` landing page template for your photo + links
-   `quarto preview` for a live local version while you edit
-   Research / publications / CV pages - a complete academic site for a graduate student

::: callout-tip
Keep your copy. In **Week 10** we push exactly this folder to GitHub and flip on GitHub Pages - it becomes `your-username.github.io`, for free.
:::

# AI-assisted coding: the principles

## "Vibe coding" and why it fails in science

::: incremental
-   A **large language model (LLM)** predicts the most *plausible* next text - including code
-   **Vibe coding** = describe, accept, run, paste the error, repeat - *without reading the code*
-   Fun for a weekend project; a problem for science:
    -   you have to **defend** every result
    -   scientific bugs are usually **silent** (wrong number, no crash)
    -   you stop **learning**
-   Our version: keep the speed, drop the blindness - **the assistant writes, you read, a tiny test decides**
:::

## The loop

::: incremental
1.  **Describe** the goal precisely - language, versions, sample input, expected output
2.  **Get** code
3.  **READ** it - every line; look up anything you don't recognize
4.  **Run** it on a tiny test you can check by hand
5.  **Check** the result against something you already know
6.  **Iterate** - paste the exact error or wrong output, say what you expected
:::

::: callout-important
Steps 3 and 5 are the ones people skip. Don't.
:::

## Where LLMs fail - the short list

::: incremental
-   **Hallucinated** functions, packages, and arguments - delivered with total confidence
-   **Outdated APIs** - last year's function names in this year's package
-   **Subtly wrong statistics** - `sd(x) / n` instead of `sd(x) / sqrt(n)`; `mean()` when you asked for `median()`
-   **Silently changing your data** - dropping every row with an `NA`, re-sorting and breaking an alignment
:::

. . .

Every failure has the same root cause - the model predicts text, it does not reason about *your* data - and the same fix: **read the code, test on an input where you know the answer**. [Ch. 18](../book/chapters/18-ai-assisted-coding.html) has worked examples of each failure and a review checklist.

## Data rules and the course policy

**Never paste into an unsupported AI tool:**

-   Unpublished data or results · human-subjects data / PHI · credentials
-   UO data classes: **green** (published data, your code) / **amber** (unpublished research, FERPA) / **red** (HIPAA). Unsupported tools: **green only**; Microsoft Copilot Chat with your UO login is covered by UO's agreement - see [UO's AI Service Offerings](https://service.uoregon.edu/TDClient/2030/Portal/KB/Article/140911/AI-Service-Offerings)

::: callout-important
**Course policy:** AI may help you learn, explore, and debug. Submitted work must be your own, you must be able to **explain every line**, and AI help gets noted in a comment or your README. Can't explain it? Don't submit it.
:::

Everything trimmed from today's slides - the chat / in-editor / agentic tool comparison, live worked examples, prompting patterns, and using assistants *to learn* - is in [Ch. 18](../book/chapters/18-ai-assisted-coding.html).

## Summary

-   **Literate programming** keeps prose, code, and results in one executable document - the practical core of reproducible, **FAIR** science
-   **Quarto** renders one `.qmd` to HTML, PDF, Word, slides, or a website; chunk options, cross-references, LaTeX math, and `.bib` citations are the same everywhere
-   The three demo files are templates for *your* work: slides for your next talk, the manuscript for your **term project report** (start it this week!), the website for Week 10
-   **AI assistants**: the assistant writes, *you read*, a tiny test decides - and nothing above green classification goes into an unsupported tool ([Ch. 18](../book/chapters/18-ai-assisted-coding.html) for the full treatment)
